extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, taxonomists, librarians, logicians, and students of classification/cataloguing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on designing and evaluating classification systems and catalogues (diagnostic keys, library catalogues, biological taxonomy), including principles for diagnostic (bifurcate) keys, selection of discriminating characters, and practical indexing strategies. Emphasises genealogical/natural classification limits, types vs classes, and the trade-offs between breadth and precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic (bifurcate) classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagnostic systems of classification should, as a general rule, be arranged on the bifurcate (dichotomous) method: choose a quality which divides the whole group into two distinct parts and subdivide each part successively by prominent, well-marked circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To refer an object use successive critical differentiae and note whether it does or does not possess each difference. Examples: Dana's crystal classification, Von Kobell's blowpipe mineral keys, Bentham's Analytical Key to the British Flora. Numerical discriminations (numbers of petals, stamens, etc.) often occur; where a bifid division is tedious, numerical criteria can be used. The method is aimed at facilitating diagnosis by successive rejection of infinite negative classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select distinctive, reliable diagnostic characters/tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose tests or characters that produce distinctive, characteristic marks of the substance or organism being diagnosed rather than tests that reproduce the whole entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (chemistry): detect potassium by producing a highly characteristic platinum-tetrachloride precipitate or flame colour, not by attempting to isolate metallic potassium. Use properties that are comparatively insoluble, produce peculiar precipitates, characteristic flame colours, or spectroscopic lines—i.e., features that reliably indicate presence even if they are otherwise of little importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification must establish useful correlations
rubrics_metrics.description: No classification or arrangement is useful unless it involves some correlation of circumstances so that knowing one thing enables the discovery of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even simple alphabetical indices are real classifications because they correlate a memorable circumstance (e.g., initial letter or author's name) with the object's place, drastically reducing search labour. Design arrangements around circumstances that commonly occur to the searcher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose catalogue keys that dwell in memory of searchers
rubrics_metrics.description: A catalogue should be arranged so that the circumstance chosen to indicate place is one most likely to be remembered by the searcher (e.g., first line of a poem, author's name).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For poetry, first line or author is most memorable; for general library use the author's name is often the best single characteristic. Select indices that correspond to typical user recall to maximise retrieval efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetical author-catalogue as primary practical scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: In a large library, classification according to the author's name (alphabetical catalogue) is the only practicable primary arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author-based alphabetical catalogues provide an exhaustive place for every name and are generally more usable than classed catalogues, which reflect one person's theoretical subdivision and often frustrate other users. Examples: British Museum catalogue; De Morgan's testimony. Anti-pattern: relying solely on a single classed catalogue without author or alphabetical access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accompany name catalogue with limited subject index
rubrics_metrics.description: A name (author) catalogue should be accompanied by a subordinate subject catalogue, but no attempt should be made to devise a theoretically complete subject classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enter every principal subject treated in a book separately under the name most likely to be used by the searcher, or under several names. Avoid trying to make a comprehensive theoretical subject taxonomy—use practical, commonly-remembered headings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise indices that produce the greatest frequent benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: Because forming multiple indices is costly, select those circumstances for indexing which will lead most frequently to the discovery of items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible useful indices include author's name, first words of title, place of publication, language, general subject. If feasible, produce multiple simple indices (the text suggests practical mechanical ways such as supplying multiple printed title slips to create alternate catalogues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not attempt impossible rigorous subject classification for books
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of books by subject into a natural, precise system is impracticable because most books treat mixed subjects and sciences are interrelated; rigorous demarcation is often impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a book on the steam-engine may be antiquarian, scientific, technical, economic, and biographical. Creating one comprehensive subject hierarchy will lead to continuous disputes about boundaries (e.g., whether Westminster Abbey belongs to architecture, church history, or English history). Use practical groupings and subordinate indices instead of forcing a single natural taxonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invest in extensive indexing/cataloguing to expand usable knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Forming extensive indices and catalogues enormously saves labour and increases available knowledge by making sources discoverable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: calendaring the State Papers, the British Museum Catalogue, the Royal Society's catalogue of memoirs. The text argues for future systematic cataloguing of large masses of historical and scientific information by government or public societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural (genealogical) classification aims to reflect descent
rubrics_metrics.description: In biology, the ultimate natural arrangement should represent genealogical descent (a tree of descent) making individuals the infimae species; classification seeks to trace descents between existing groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a system ought ideally to represent descent of each individual form and be extremely detailed, but practical limits force stopping at convenient points. Natural classification is most instructive for living things because of hereditary relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise limits of genealogical classification for non-biological domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Genealogical or natural classification principles appropriate in biology need not be best for mineralogy, chemistry, astronomy, or practical purposes; different purposes may demand other correlations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: minerals do not have hereditary descent; for practical or legal needs (e.g., medicinal classification, legal treatment of whales), groupings that correlate useful properties or legal definitions may be preferable to strict genealogical groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for gradation, transition, and exceptions in natural groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Where gradation of characters and intermediate forms exist, precise demarcation between groups is often impossible; classifiers must define and register degrees and limits of gradation rather than force sharp boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin's observation: if intermediate ranks have not been extinguished, they bar absolutely distinct definitions. When gradation exists, mark extreme limits of family relationship or select the most generalized representative as type; accept that natural arrangement may lack strong lines of demarcation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types must be abstracted into classes by specifying shared qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification by types (selecting a typical specimen and grouping around it) is not truly distinct logically; to make it a class one must abstract from the type a finite number of qualities that other objects may resemble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A type is an individual; no other object exactly matches it. If types are used without abstracting shared properties, classification is inconsistent. Practical consequence: either tighten definitions so all included forms possess specified marks, or accept anomalous genera/latitude in definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance definition specificity to avoid over-breadth or anomalous genera
rubrics_metrics.description: When forming class definitions, there is a trade-off: too few marks (overly broad) will include too many forms; too many marks (overly narrow) will create anomalous genera which approximate the class but fail in particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, naturalists often allow considerable latitude in order definitions; but this implies either reassigning borderline genera or recognising that exceptions effectively constitute new classes. Be explicit about allowed variation and the intended scope of the class.
